Partnership for Innovation and Empowerment | 1310 Eastern Avenue NE, Washington, DC  20019 | pieus.org  
 
June 15, 2026 
 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 
Department of Health and Human Services 
Submitted via Regulations.gov | Docket No. CMS-0062-P 
 
Re: Comments in Support of the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior 
Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) 
Dear Administrator Oz and Members of the CMS Team: 
My name is Brady J. Buckner, and I am President of the Partnership for Innovation and 
Empowerment (PIE), a 501c3 Nonprofit. PIE works directly with Black and low-income 
communities, and healthcare access is one of the most persistent issues we hear about from 
the people we serve. We have sat in rooms with community members who described the same 
experience over and over: their doctor prescribed a medication, and then they waited. And 
waited. And sometimes they just never got it. (source) 
That is why we are writing today to express our strong support for this proposed rule and to offer 
several recommendations for strengthening it. 
I. Electronic Prior Authorization: We Are Fully Behind It 
PIE supports CMS's proposal to require electronic prior authorization (ePA) for medications 
across both the medical and pharmacy benefit. (source) Right now, prior authorization for many 
drugs still runs on phone calls, faxes, and paper forms. That is a problem for any provider, but it 
is a much bigger problem for the community health centers and small practices serving low-
income and minority patients, who simply do not have the staff or systems to fight a slow, 
outdated bureaucracy. 
Giving providers real-time access to coverage information, letting them submit PAs 
electronically, and allowing them to track request status is not just a technology upgrade. It is a 
fairness issue. We urge CMS to finalize this requirement and to provide real technical support 
for smaller, safety-net providers during the rollout. 
II. Timelines and Denial Justifications: Go Further 
PIE recommends that CMS require prior authorization decisions within 24 hours for all drugs, 
not just urgent requests. (source) The proposed 72-hour window for standard cases is an 
improvement, but it is still too long for people who cannot afford to miss doses or delay 
treatment. A three-day wait can mean a missed work shift, a health crisis, or an emergency 
room visit that ends up costing far more than the medication ever would have. 
 
The Financial Services Innovation Coalition | Washington, DC | fsicoalition.org 
We want to be direct about something: faster timelines only mean something if the decisions are 
fair. We are asking CMS to put real oversight in place to make sure that speed requirements are 
not being used to push through denials. That is a real risk and CMS should be watching for it 
closely. 
 
On denials: PIE strongly recommends that CMS require a detailed, plain-language justification 
for every denial, including initial denials, delivered to both the provider and the patient at the 
same time. (source) Vague denial letters leave families with no idea what happened or what 
they can do about it. People deserve to know exactly why a request was denied and what their 
next steps are. Anything less is bureaucratic cover, not transparency. 
III. Payer Reporting Metrics: Make the Data Mean Something 
We support requiring payers to report prior authorization metrics, and we want CMS to push 
further. (source) 
Reporting on API usage alone does not tell us whether patients are actually getting the 
medications they need. We recommend that API usage data be paired with real patient and 
provider experience data, including denial rates, appeal overturn rates, and the average time 
from PA request to treatment. CMS should publish this information in a meaningful annual 
public report that advocates and policymakers can actually use. 
Medicare Part D plans should also be required to publicly report PA metrics, just like other 
payers subject to this rule. (source) Those metrics should be broken out at the plan level across 
all markets, with specific data on brand versus generic drugs, by therapeutic area, and with 
separate figures on initial denials and step therapy. Aggregated data lets disparities hide. We 
need the details. 
IV. Step Therapy: Our Communities Cannot Afford Another Round of Delays 
Step therapy, which requires patients to try and fail on cheaper alternatives before getting the 
medication their doctor already prescribed, is harmful policy. It is especially harmful for the 
communities we work with, where healthcare delays already compound existing health 
disparities. (source) 
We urge CMS not to permit Medicare Advantage plans to use step therapy, and to collect and 
publicly release data on how MA plans are currently using prior authorization for Part B drugs so 
the full picture is visible. 
We also strongly recommend that CMS require plans to honor step therapy completion across 
plan changes. If a patient has already been through the required steps to access their 
medication, they should not have to start over just because their insurance changed. That reset 
serves no legitimate clinical purpose. (source) 
Finally, payers should be required to clearly disclose their step therapy requirements, not bury 
them inside prior authorization processes. And there must be a real appeals and exceptions 
process in place that patients can actually navigate. 
 
The Financial Services Innovation Coalition | Washington, DC | fsicoalition.org 
Conclusion 
This proposed rule is one of the most meaningful steps CMS has taken toward making 
healthcare work for people who have historically been left behind by the system. PIE urges 
CMS to finalize it and to take the additional recommendations above seriously. The families we 
work with are counting on it. (source) 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
Brady J. Buckner 
President 
Partnership for Innovation and Empowerment (PIE) 
202-680-4749 
bbuckner@pieus.org
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Brady J. Buckner, President, Partnership for Innovation and Empowerment (PIE)
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group / nonprofit community organization
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** PIE is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit working directly with Black and low-income communities; healthcare access is described as a persistent community issue.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

PIE strongly supports CMS-0062-P as a fairness and health equity reform that can modernize PA for drugs and reduce delays for low-income and minority patients. It asks CMS to finalize ePA for medical and pharmacy benefit drugs, require 24-hour decisions for all drugs, strengthen plain-language denial notices, expand meaningful public reporting, and address step therapy harms.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** None specifically cited beyond CMS-0062-P.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization; APIs generally; no named FHIR IG or NCPDP standard cited.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization for drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Current PA relies on phone calls, faxes, and paper forms, disproportionately burdening community health centers and small practices serving low-income and minority patients.
- **Specific request:** Finalize ePA across medical and pharmacy benefits, enable real-time coverage information, electronic submission, and status tracking, and provide technical support for smaller safety-net providers.

**Topic 2: Drug PA decision timelines and oversight**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** A 72-hour standard timeframe remains too long for people who cannot afford missed doses, work disruptions, health crises, or avoidable emergency care.
- **Specific request:** Require PA decisions within 24 hours for all drugs and monitor whether faster decision rules are being used to accelerate denials.

**Topic 3: Denial justifications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify / strengthen
- **Rationale:** Vague denials leave families and providers without actionable information for appeals or corrections.
- **Specific request:** Require detailed, plain-language justifications for every denial, including initial denials, delivered simultaneously to provider and patient.

**Topic 4: Payer reporting and public transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** API usage alone does not show whether patients receive medications; aggregate reporting can hide disparities.
- **Specific request:** Pair API usage data with patient/provider experience metrics, denial rates, appeal overturn rates, and time from PA request to treatment; publish a useful annual public report; require Medicare Part D plan-level public PA metrics broken out by market, brand/generic, therapeutic area, initial denials, and step therapy.

**Topic 5: Step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Oppose harmful uses / modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy forces patients to fail on cheaper alternatives and compounds disparities.
- **Specific request:** Do not permit MA plans to use step therapy; collect and release data on MA Part B drug PA use; require plans to honor completed step therapy across plan changes; require clear disclosure and navigable appeals/exceptions.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12/S14:** Supports ePA implementation across both benefit channels and asks CMS to support smaller safety-net providers.
- **S16/S17:** Requests detailed, plain-language denial reasons for every denial, including initial denials, delivered to patients and providers.
- **S20/S43:** Requests 24-hour decisions for all drug PA requests, not only urgent cases.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Requests API usage metrics paired with patient- and provider-experience measures, denial/appeal rates, and annual public reporting.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to step therapy RFI topics by opposing MA step therapy, supporting data transparency, portability of completed steps, disclosure, and accessible exceptions.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize ePA requirements for medications across medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Provide real technical support to smaller and safety-net providers.
3. Require PA decisions within 24 hours for all drugs.
4. Monitor denials to ensure faster timelines do not increase unfair denial rates.
5. Require detailed plain-language denial reasons for every denial and send them to both patient and provider.
6. Publish annual public metrics that include denial rates, appeal overturn rates, and time from request to treatment.
7. Require Medicare Part D plan-level public PA metrics with meaningful breakouts.
8. Prohibit MA step therapy or, at minimum, require transparent data and patient protections.
9. Require portability of completed step therapy across plan changes.
10. Require clear disclosure and usable appeals/exceptions for step therapy.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Delayed medication access, inequitable burden on Black and low-income communities, vague denial letters, inadequate reporting granularity, and step therapy delays.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Missed doses, missed work, health crises, emergency visits, denied care, and hidden disparities.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Safety-net providers' limited staff and systems; outdated paper/fax/phone workflows.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** No specific numeric studies cited; the comment uses community experience and placeholder source markers.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None identified by name.
- **Examples provided:** Community members prescribed medication and then waiting indefinitely; step therapy resets after plan changes.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Black and low-income communities, patients, community health centers, small practices, safety-net providers, Medicare Part D enrollees, MA enrollees, advocates, and policymakers.
- **Economic implications:** Faster and fairer PA may avoid missed work and emergency room costs; reporting may expose disparities.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports ePA and real-time information but requests technical support for smaller providers.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if it reduces waiting, improves transparency, prevents step therapy resets, and enables access to prescribed medications.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with requests for stronger patient protections
- **Tone:** Advocacy-focused, direct, equity-centered
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Giving providers real-time access to coverage information... is not just a technology upgrade. It is a fairness issue." - Context: Support for ePA.
2. "A three-day wait can mean a missed work shift, a health crisis, or an emergency room visit..." - Context: Request for 24-hour drug PA decisions.
3. "Aggregated data lets disparities hide. We need the details." - Context: Reporting metrics.
4. "That reset serves no legitimate clinical purpose." - Context: Requiring patients to repeat step therapy after plan changes.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Requests 24-hour decisions for all drugs and real rollout support.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Notes limited staff and systems among safety-net providers and economic consequences for patients.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on phone/fax/paper burden for small practices and CHCs.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Central theme involving Black and low-income communities.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports ePA but asks for technical support.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not addressed in standards detail.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Main concern is timely medication access.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Limited to provider support and CMS oversight.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Supports ePA across both benefit pathways.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong focus on denials, public reporting, and step therapy disclosure.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Critiques phone, fax, paper, and opaque step therapy processes.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed.
